meta.title: Hebrew A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Hebrew → English (see the Hebrew, recall the meaning) and English → Hebrew (see an English meaning, recall the Hebrew). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. The Hebrew taught is the modern standard language of Israel. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Hebrew, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 311 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, introducing yourself, family, numbers, telling the time, the days of the week, food and drink, shopping and money, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, and the pronouns, question words, prepositions and conjunctions every sentence is built out of — and the other 189 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Hebrew, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word: every form of a noun or a verb added together, including the forms written with a prefix such as ו "and", ה "the" or ב "in" joined to the front. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword is printed as Hebrew is normally written — without vowel points, in the full spelling — with the POINTED form beneath it, which shows how it is said, and Wiktionary's romanisation with the stress marked (shalóm, katáv). Words spelt alike are separate cards where the level teaches both (שֵׁם "name", שָׁם "there"). The Hebrew Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the letters and the vowel points. The 181 nouns show their gender and plural; the 119 verbs are given, as Hebrew dictionaries give them, in the past tense "he" form, with their infinitive, present, future and binyan (the verb pattern) beside them and, behind the All forms fold, their past, present, future and imperative by person. Real example sentences come with 499 of the 500 words, three apiece for 499 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, forms, pointing and romanisation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
